claims.text: High configurational entropy predicts intrinsic thermal stability in nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA.
Surface-energy dominance and non-isothermal cycling compromise the intrinsic thermal stability of HENA.
HENA undergo accelerated phase separation at substantially lower temperatures than bulk alloys of the same composition.
Elevated-temperature exposure of HENA nucleates B2 or Laves intermetallic phases.
B2 and Laves secondary phases are intrinsically brittle.
Particles smaller than 50 nm have sufficiently high surface-to-volume ratios to maximize surface-energy contributions.
A high surface-to-volume ratio reduces the effective activation energy for atomic diffusion and phase separation.
Non-isothermal cycling introduces kinetic instabilities that are absent under static bulk conditions.
Bulk HEAs rely on sluggish diffusion to stabilize their solid-solution structures.
Nanoparticle surface energy lowers the thermodynamic barrier to phase separation.
B2 or Laves phases that are avoided in bulk designs become energetically favorable at the nanoscale.
Formation of brittle intermetallic phases will sharply reduce the mechanical integrity of the nanoparticles.
Elevated-temperature structural evolution may cause nanoparticle agglomeration.
The single BCC phase of NbTaTiV remains stable up to 900°C.
W-Ta-V-Cr maintains single-phase stability up to 900°C or higher.
Surface effects become negligible for particles larger than 200 nm.
Some elemental combinations can inherently suppress intermetallic formation at the nanoscale because their mixing entropy cannot be overcome by surface energy.
Direct elevated-temperature stability data are lacking for five-component equiatomic HEA nanoparticles.
Most relevant studies focus on bulk alloys or room-temperature mechanical behavior rather than nanoparticle stability at elevated temperature.
The particle-size or temperature threshold at which surface energy overcomes configurational entropy is unknown.

contradictions.description: The target material is repeatedly defined as a five-transition-metal nanoparticle, but NbTaTiV and W-Ta-V-Cr are proposed as experimental variants even though each contains only four elements.
